text: Most land animals can paddle across a river, and many dinosaurs probably could too. Footprints scratched into old riverbeds show dinosaurs touching the bottom with their toes while floating.
The famous "sea monsters" like [[@marine-reptiles-plesiosaur|plesiosaurs]] were [[reptile|reptiles]], but not dinosaurs.
Spinosaurus is the big puzzle. Scientists disagree about how much time it spent in water. And today, the champion swimming dinosaurs are [[@penguins-cold|penguins]], which are birds.

sec.t:
During the [[@dino-age-span|age of dinosaurs]], the seas were ruled by other reptiles. Ichthyosaurs looked like dolphins. Plesiosaurs had small heads, [[@sauropod-necks|long necks]] and four big flippers. Mosasaurs were giant swimming lizards related to today's monitor lizards.

None of them were dinosaurs. Scientists define dinosaurs by features of the hips and legs that let them stand upright on land. Sea reptiles came from different branches of the reptile family tree, and they moved to the sea on their own.

In 2007, scientists described an unusual trackway in La Rioja, Spain. Instead of full footprints, the rock showed long scratch marks in pairs, left by the claws of a two-legged meat-eater. The animal was floating in water and kicking off the bottom, the way you might "walk" in a swimming pool on tiptoe.

Similar swim tracks have been found at St. George, in Utah, and in China. They show that some meat-eating dinosaurs were happy to cross rivers and lakes. That does not make them true swimmers, but it means water was no barrier.

sec.h: A diving bird in the dinosaur age
sec.t:
Some dinosaurs really did become expert swimmers. Hesperornis was a flightless bird that lived about 80 million years ago in a shallow sea that then covered the middle of North America. Its fossils have been found in Kansas.

It had tiny useless wings, teeth in its beak and powerful legs set far back, like a modern diving bird. It probably chased fish underwater, kicking with its feet, rather like a loon or grebe today.

Penguins "fly" underwater using their stiff wings as flippers. [[@ocean-penguins-swim|Emperor penguins]] can dive deeper than 500 m. Ducks paddle, cormorants dive after fish, and gannets plunge into the sea from high above. Even the ancestors of whales and [[@dolphins-click|dolphins]] took to the water from land, though they were [[mammal|mammals]], not dinosaurs. Swimming has [[evolve|evolved]] again and again, which is why many scientists expect a few more dinosaurs to turn out to have been at home in water.

text: Earth's crust, its rocky outer skin, is surprisingly thin. Under the oceans it is only about 5 to 10 kilometres thick, roughly the distance a Mumbai local train covers in ten minutes. Under the continents it is thicker, usually 30 to 50 kilometres, and up to about 70 kilometres under the Himalaya and Tibet.

Compared to the whole planet, that is very little. Earth's radius is about 6,371 kilometres, so the crust makes up only about one per cent of its volume. Below it lies the [[mantle|mantle]], a thick layer of hot rock, and then the core. Everything we have ever mined, drilled or built sits in that thin top layer.

st.reveal: Continental crust is usually 30 to 50 km thick, and much thicker under big mountains. Oceanic crust is only about 5 to 10 km thick, but it is made of heavier rock, which is why it sits lower and the oceans fill the space above it.

sec.t:
The crust under the oceans is mostly [[basalt|basalt]], a dark, heavy volcanic rock. It forms at ridges in the middle of the oceans, where melted rock rises and cools. It is young by Earth standards. The oldest parts are less than about 200 million years old.

Continental crust is thicker but lighter. It is mostly made of rocks like [[granite|granite]], full of light-coloured minerals. Because it is light, it floats higher on the mantle, a bit like a big block of wood floats higher than a thin one. That is why continents stand above the sea. Some continental rocks are about 4 billion years old.

People have tried to drill down to the Moho. In 1970, Soviet scientists started the Kola Superdeep Borehole in the far north of Russia. By 1989 it reached about 12.3 kilometres, deeper than Mount Everest is tall. At the bottom the rock was about 180°C, much hotter than expected, and drilling became too hard.

The hole is only about 23 centimetres wide and is now capped with a rusty metal lid. Even so, it went only about a third of the way through the crust there. Scientists in Japan have a ship called Chikyu designed to drill into thin ocean crust, hoping to one day reach the mantle.

Crust is thickest under big mountain ranges. When India's [[plate|plate]] pushed into Asia, the crust crumpled and stacked up, raising the [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]]. Just as an iceberg has a big chunk hidden underwater, high mountains have deep roots of crust pushing down into the mantle.

That is why the crust under Tibet is about twice as thick as under most continents. The roots also help hold the mountains up.

The crust is not one solid piece. Together with the top of the mantle, it is broken into giant plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Where plates pull apart, new crust forms. Where they collide, crust gets pushed down, crumpled into mountains or melted in [[@volcano|volcanoes]].

So the ground under your feet is moving right now, though far too slowly to feel. Over millions of years, that slow motion has opened oceans, closed them again and carried India all the way from near Antarctica to Asia.

sec.t:
[[@thunderstorms|ఉరుముల మబ్బు]] అంటే పైకి లేస్తున్న గాలితో ఏర్పడిన ఒక గోపురం. అది తరచుగా 10 కి.మీ. కంటే ఎక్కువ ఎత్తు ఉంటుంది. పైభాగంలో నీరు గడ్డకట్టే స్థాయి కంటే చాలా చల్లగా ఉంటుంది. చిన్న చిన్న మంచు [[crystal|స్ఫటికాలు]] పైకి ఎగురుతుంటాయి. బరువైన మెత్తటి వడగళ్ల ముక్కలు వాటి మధ్యలోంచి కిందికి పడుతుంటాయి. అవి ఒకదాన్నొకటి రాసుకుంటూ వెళ్లినప్పుడు విద్యుత్ ఆవేశం రాలిపోతుంది. తివాచీ మీద కాళ్లు ఈడ్చుకుంటూ నడిచినప్పుడు వచ్చే [[@static-electricity|స్థిర విద్యుత్]] లాగే.

ధన ఆవేశం ఉన్న తేలికైన మంచు స్ఫటికాలు మబ్బు పైభాగంలో చేరతాయి. రుణ ఆవేశం ఉన్న బరువైన ముక్కలు కింది భాగంలో పోగవుతాయి. కొద్దిసేపట్లోనే మబ్బు ఒక పెద్ద బ్యాటరీలా తయారవుతుంది. దాని భాగాలకూ నేలకూ మధ్య పదుల కోట్ల వోల్టులు ఉంటాయి.

మామూలుగా గాలి కరెంటును పారనివ్వదు. కానీ ఆవేశం బాగా బలపడినప్పుడు, ‘లీడర్’ అనే మసకగా, కొమ్మలు కొమ్మలుగా ఉండే దారి మబ్బు నుంచి మెట్లు మెట్లుగా వంకరటింకరగా కిందికి దిగుతుంది. అది నేలకు దగ్గరయ్యాక, ఒక చెట్టు నుంచో, స్తంభం నుంచో, భవనం నుంచో ఒక నిప్పురవ్వ దాన్ని కలవడానికి పైకి దూసుకెళ్తుంది. దారి పూర్తవుతుంది.

అప్పుడు ఆ దారి వెంట భారీ [[current|విద్యుత్ ప్రవాహం]] పరుగెత్తుతుంది. మనకు కనిపించే మెరుపు వెలుగు అదే. ఒక సెకను లోపే చాలా దెబ్బలు అదే దారిలో కిందికి దిగుతాయి కాబట్టి, మెరుపు తరచుగా మిణుకుమిణుకుమంటుంది. అయితే చాలా మెరుపులు అసలు నేలను తాకనే తాకవు. మబ్బు లోపలే, లేదా మబ్బుల మధ్యే దూకుతాయి.

మెరుపు ఆ దారిలోని గాలిని కొన్ని మైక్రోసెకన్లలోనే (ఒక మైక్రోసెకను అంటే సెకనులో పది లక్షో వంతు) సుమారు 30,000 °C దాకా వేడెక్కిస్తుంది. గాలి ఎంత వేగంగా వ్యాకోచిస్తుందంటే, అది ఒక షాక్ వేవ్‌ను సృష్టిస్తుంది. అదే మనకు [[@thunder-sound|ఉరుముగా]] వినిపిస్తుంది. వెలుగు దాదాపు వెంటనే నిన్ను చేరుతుంది. కానీ శబ్దం 3 సెకన్లలో సుమారు 1 కి.మీ. మాత్రమే ప్రయాణిస్తుంది. ఆ తేడాతోనే తుఫాను ఎంత దూరంలో ఉందో తెలుస్తుంది.

text: A waterfall forms where a river suddenly drops over a steep step. Most often, the river flows over a layer of hard rock lying on top of softer rock. The water wears the soft rock away faster, and a step appears. Water tumbling over the edge digs a deep hole at the bottom, called a plunge pool, and scoops out the soft rock behind the falls.

Eventually the hard ledge on top is left hanging with nothing underneath. It breaks off, and the waterfall moves a little upstream. Over thousands of years, this repeats again and again, leaving a deep, narrow gorge downstream. [[glacier|Glaciers]], earthquakes and volcanoes can make waterfalls too.

st.reveal: Falling water eats away the soft rock at the base, until the hard ledge above breaks off. Each collapse moves the edge a little further upstream, leaving a gorge behind.

sec.t:
Rivers carry sand and stones that scrape at their beds, wearing them down. But different [[@rocks-types|rocks]] wear away at different speeds. Hard rocks like sandstone, [[granite|granite]] or limestone resist. Soft rocks like shale crumble easily.

When a river crosses from hard rock onto soft, the soft part erodes faster and drops lower. The water falls further each year, so it hits harder and digs deeper, speeding up the process. The spray splashes back against the cliff, and the soft rock behind the curtain of water wears away into a hollow. Some waterfalls have a gap behind them big enough to walk into, with a curtain of water roaring past your nose.

[[@niagara-falls|Niagara Falls]], on the border of the USA and Canada, formed about 12,000 years ago, when the ice sheets of the last ice age melted. A thick layer of hard dolostone sits on top of soft shale. The river has been chewing through it ever since.

The falls have moved about 11 km upstream, leaving the Niagara Gorge behind. In the past they retreated around a metre a year. Today, much of the river is sent through tunnels to power stations before it reaches the edge, which has slowed the [[erosion|erosion]] to a fraction of that.

In 1969, engineers built a temporary dam to stop the water flowing over the smaller American Falls. For several months, visitors could walk on the dry riverbed and look at the bare cliff. Engineers decided against trying to tidy away the fallen boulders at its foot.

sec.h: Other ways to make a waterfall
sec.t:
[[@glaciers|Glaciers]] are powerful diggers. A big glacier carves a deep valley, while smaller side glaciers carve shallower ones. When the ice melts, the small valleys are left hanging high above the main one, and their streams pour over the edge. Yosemite Falls in California and many waterfalls in Norway formed this way.

Earthquake faults can lift one block of land above another. [[lava|Lava]] flows can harden into steps of rock. At the coast, streams sometimes tumble straight off cliffs into the sea.

The tallest waterfall on Earth, Angel Falls in Venezuela, drops about 979 m from a flat-topped mountain. The widest curtain of falling water belongs to [[@victoria-falls|Victoria Falls]], on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, more than 1.7 km across.

Many of India's best waterfalls roar during the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] and shrink to a trickle in the dry months. In the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], Jog Falls in Karnataka drops about 253 m in four streams. Dudhsagar, on the Goa–Karnataka border, falls more than 300 m, and trains cross a bridge right in front of it. In [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]], one of the rainiest places on Earth, Nohkalikai Falls plunges about 340 m into a turquoise pool.

Falling water also carries energy. In 1902, a power station at Shivanasamudra Falls in Karnataka began sending electricity to the Kolar gold mines, one of the earliest big [[hydroelectric|hydroelectric]] plants in Asia.

text: Spacecraft have landed in many parts of the Moon's near side, the half that always faces Earth, and more recently on the [[@moon-far-side|far side]] and near the south pole.

The first soft landing, meaning a landing gentle enough to survive, was the Soviet Union's Luna 9 in February 1966. Between 1969 and 1972, six American Apollo missions put 12 astronauts on the Moon. China landed the first spacecraft on the far side in 2019. In August 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 landed closer to the south pole than any mission before it.
By the end of 2025, five countries had made soft landings: the Soviet Union, the USA, China, India and Japan. Private companies have started landing too.

sec.t:
Landing on the Moon is hard. There is no air, so [[@parachutes|parachutes]] don't work, and a spacecraft has to slow itself down using rockets alone. Many early attempts crashed.

The [[@space-race|space race]] between the USA and the Soviet Union pushed both countries to try again and again. After Luna 9, the US Surveyor 1 landed a few months later. Both sent back pictures showing that the surface was firm enough to stand on.

Then, on 20 July 1969, Apollo 11 touched down on a flat plain called the Sea of Tranquillity. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to walk on the Moon. Five more crewed landings followed. The last, Apollo 17 in December 1972, landed in a valley called Taurus-Littrow, and nobody has walked on the Moon since.

{{story:space-race}}

The Soviet Union chose [[@robots|robots]]. In 1970, Luna 16 scooped up Moon soil and flew it back to Earth without any astronauts. The same year, Luna 17 delivered Lunokhod 1, a remote-controlled [[rover|rover]] that looked like a bathtub on eight wheels. Drivers on Earth steered it for about ten months and covered around 10 km, sending back thousands of pictures. They had to drive with a delay of a few seconds, since radio signals take time to cross the gap to the Moon and back. In 1973, Lunokhod 2 drove about 39 km, a distance record on another world that lasted until a Mars rover beat it in 2014.

For almost 40 years after 1976, no spacecraft made a soft landing on the Moon. Then China's Chang'e 3 landed in 2013. Chang'e 4 made history in 2019 by landing in Von Kármán [[crater|crater]] on the far side, which is impossible to see from Earth. China later brought back soil from the near side in 2020, and from the far side in 2024, a first.

India's first attempt, Chandrayaan-2's Vikram lander, crashed in 2019. Four years later, [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]] landed safely on 23 August 2023, at about 69 degrees south. India named the spot Shiv Shakti point, and 23 August is now celebrated as National Space Day. The rover Pragyan drove around and measured the soil.

In January 2024, Japan's SLIM lander touched down within about 100 m of its target, though it tipped onto its nose.

In February 2024, the American company Intuitive Machines landed Odysseus near the south pole, the first privately built spacecraft to land on the Moon. It landed tilted on its side but still sent back data. In March 2025, another company, Firefly Aerospace, set its Blue Ghost lander down upright and working.

Several other landers, from Israel, Russia and a Japanese company, crashed in recent years. Each failure taught engineers something about one of the hardest parts of any space mission: the last few kilometres.

Every landing site is a kind of museum. The bottom halves of the six Apollo landers, three moon buggies, scientific instruments and dozens of objects remain where they were left. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed them from [[orbit|orbit]], and its pictures even show the dark trails where astronauts walked. With no wind or rain, those [[@spacesuits|spacesuit]] bootprints could last for millions of years.

text: A kite stays up because it is tilted against the wind, like a wing. As the wind hits the tilted kite, the air is pushed downwards and backwards. The air pushes back on the kite, upwards and backwards. The upward part of that push is called [[lift|lift]].

The string is the secret. It holds the kite at just the right [[@geometry-everyday|angle]] and stops it simply blowing away. Without the string, the wind would carry the kite along like a leaf. With it, the kite climbs into the wind instead. When lift and the pull of the string balance the kite's weight and the wind's push, it hangs steady in the sky.

sec.t:
Four forces act on a flying kite. Weight pulls it down. Wind pushes it back, a force called drag. Lift pushes it up. The string pulls it down and towards the flyer.

If the kite is flat to the ground, it gets almost no lift. If it faces the wind straight on, it gets lots of drag and little lift, so it just gets shoved backwards. The best angle is in between. That's why kites have a bridle, the short strings that attach to the main line. Moving where it's tied changes the angle.

Wind matters too. Too little, and the kite sinks. Too much, and the string may snap. Higher up, winds are usually steadier and stronger, which is why kites often fly better once they get above the treetops.

Kites were [[@ancient-china|invented in China]] more than 2,000 years ago, possibly first made of silk and bamboo. Paper kites came later. They spread across Asia, including India, and much later to Europe.

The bird and the toy share a name in English. A kite hangs on the wind with hardly a flap, just like the [[@kites-birds|black kite]] that circles over Indian cities.

Before they built their aeroplane, the [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]] flew a large kite in 1899 to test their idea of twisting wings to steer. In 1901, the Italian inventor Guglielmo Marconi used a kite in Newfoundland, now part of Canada, to lift a long wire aerial high into the air. With it, he picked up a faint radio signal sent from England, across the Atlantic Ocean.

Benjamin Franklin's famous [[@lightning-rods|kite experiment]] of 1752 showed that [[@lightning|lightning]] is electricity. Some historians are not sure it happened exactly as described. Either way, it was extremely dangerous. Don't try it.

Each January, around Makar Sankranti, rooftops across Gujarat and Rajasthan fill with families flying kites. In [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]], the International Kite Festival draws flyers from many countries. In Delhi, Independence Day on 15 August is a big kite-flying day.

In the USA, Washington, D.C., holds a kite festival near the Washington Monument each spring. Different places, same idea: a scrap of paper, a stick or two, a string, and the wind.

text: House sparrows haven't vanished everywhere. In many villages and small towns in India, they are still common. But in big cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad and Kolkata, their numbers have dropped sharply over the last few decades. The same thing has happened in cities like London.

Scientists think several changes in modern cities are to blame, working together. New buildings leave sparrows few places to nest. Tidier gardens and fewer insects make it hard to feed chicks. Less grain is spilled in the open. Which cause matters most is still debated.

sec.h: A bird that lives with people
sec.t:
The house sparrow has lived alongside humans for thousands of years, probably ever since people began farming and storing grain. In India, sparrows nested in gaps in walls, behind photo frames, inside ceiling fan cups and under tiled roofs. Many grandparents remember sparrows hopping inside their homes, picking up spilled rice.

Sparrows are small, about 15 cm long. Males have a grey cap and a black bib. Females are plain brown and buff. They chirp constantly, which is one reason people noticed when the chirping stopped.

In 2020, a large report called the State of India's Birds used millions of sightings sent in by birdwatchers. It found that house sparrow numbers across India as a whole had been roughly stable over the long term. The steep drops were in the biggest cities.

So the real story is less "the sparrow is disappearing" and more "the sparrow is leaving big cities". As [[@cities-grow|cities grow]], the way they are built makes a difference to which birds can live in them.

In 1958, China's government launched a campaign against pests, and sparrows were on the list because they ate grain. Millions of people banged pots and pans to keep sparrows flying until they dropped from exhaustion. Sparrow numbers crashed.

But sparrows also eat insects. Without them, locusts and other crop pests increased. The campaign is often linked to the damage to harvests in the terrible [[famine|famine]] that followed. Sparrows were soon taken off the list.

House sparrows are not native to the Americas. In 1851 and 1852, people released them in Brooklyn, [[@new-york|New York]], hoping they would eat caterpillars damaging trees. They spread across almost all of North America within about 50 years. Today many Americans see them as pests, because they compete with native birds such as bluebirds for nest holes.

Since 2010, people around the world have marked World Sparrow Day on 20 March. The idea started in India with a conservationist named Mohammed Dilawar. In 2012, Delhi made the house sparrow its state bird. Bihar has it as its state bird too.

You can help. Wooden nest boxes, native plants that attract insects such as [[@butterflies-life|butterflies]] and their caterpillars, and a shallow dish of water all make a city friendlier. Families across India have put up boxes, and sparrows often move in within a season.

text: Rainwater harvesting means catching rain where it falls instead of letting it run into drains. In most systems, the rain lands on a roof, flows through gutters and pipes, and is filtered to remove leaves and dirt. Then it goes one of two ways.

It can be stored in a tank and used for washing, gardening or [[@how-water-tank-overflow|flushing toilets]]. Or it can be sent down into the ground through a pit or an old well, where it soaks in and refills the [[@groundwater|groundwater]] that wells and borewells draw from. Many homes and schools in India do both. It is an old idea that has become important again as cities grow and wells run dry.

sec.t:
The calculation is simple. One millimetre of rain on one square metre gives one litre of water. Chennai gets roughly 1,400 mm of rain in an average year. A roof of 100 square metres, a little bigger than a badminton court, could catch about 1.4 lakh litres.

Not all of it can be saved. Some splashes away or evaporates, and the first rain of the season is usually thrown away because it washes off a dirty roof. Even so, a well-built system can save most of what falls. During heavy [[@monsoon|monsoon]] storms, that also means less water flooding the streets.

People in India were harvesting rain long before pipes and pumps. In the Thar Desert, families built *kunds*, round underground tanks with a sloping catchment around them, to store rain for the dry months. Tamil Nadu has thousands of old [[irrigation|irrigation]] tanks called *eris*. In Gujarat and Rajasthan, people built grand [[@stepwells|stepwells]] to reach water stored in the ground.

In the 1980s and 1990s, villagers in the Alwar district of Rajasthan, working with an organisation led by [[@india-water-man|Rajendra Singh]], repaired and built hundreds of small earthen dams called *johads*. These hold rainwater long enough for it to soak in. Local streams that had dried up began to flow again for more of the year.

[[@chennai|Chennai]] has no big river to rely on, and its groundwater was falling fast. In 2003, Tamil Nadu made rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for buildings. Many people saw water levels in their wells rise in the years that followed.

But rules only work if systems are looked after. In 2019, after weak rains, Chennai's main [[reservoir|reservoirs]] almost dried up and the city depended on tankers and even a water train. That crisis pushed many families to repair old pits and clean blocked filters.

In parts of the USA, rainwater laws can surprise people. In Colorado, where rivers are shared out by strict water rights, homes were only allowed to use rain barrels from 2016, and only two barrels each. Texas, on the other hand, encourages rain harvesting with tax breaks.

Cities from Bengaluru to Berlin now ask new buildings to catch rain. Each roof only adds a little. But when thousands of roofs send rain into the ground, the water that feeds a neighbourhood's [[@wells-borewells|borewells]] can slowly start to rise.

text: All paint has two main parts. The first is a [[pigment|pigment]], a powder that gives the colour. The second is a binder, a sticky liquid that holds the powder together and glues it to the surface. Change the binder and you get a different kind of paint.

Brushes are simpler. They are bundles of animal hair or plastic fibres, squeezed into a metal collar and fixed to a wooden handle. The kind of hair decides how the brush behaves: stiff and scratchy, or soft and springy.

sec.h: Colours from rocks, plants and bugs
sec.t:
The oldest pigments came from the ground. [[@cave-art|Cave painters]] used red and yellow [[ochre|ochre]], which are earth coloured by iron, and black from charcoal. In India, the painters of the [[@ajanta-colours|Ajanta caves]] used earth colours, soot and, for some blues, lapis lazuli.

Some colours were very hard to get. Ultramarine blue came from lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan and carried west along trade routes, and in [[@renaissance|Renaissance]] Europe it was often kept for the robes of the most important figures. Other pigments came from plants, or even insects: carmine red is made from tiny cochineal bugs that live on cactus.

Many old pigments were also dangerous. Some whites contained lead, and a bright green once made with arsenic was used in wallpaper. Modern paints for children are made to be much safer.

The binder changes everything. Egg yolk makes tempera, which [[medieval|medieval]] painters used. Linseed oil, pressed from flax seeds, makes oil paint, which dries slowly so artists can blend colours for days. Gum arabic, from acacia trees, makes watercolour. Acrylic paint, which appeared in the mid-1900s, uses a kind of [[@plastic-made|plastic]] that dries quickly and becomes waterproof.

For a long time, painters mixed their own paints and stored them in pigs' bladders tied with string. In 1841, an American painter named John Goffe Rand patented a squeezable metal tube. Paint could now be carried easily, and painting outdoors became much simpler, which suited the [[@impressionism|Impressionists]] who loved painting in natural light.

Brushes for oil paint are often made from hog bristles, which are stiff enough to push thick paint around. Soft watercolour brushes are made from fine hairs, such as sable, which hold lots of water and come to a sharp point. Today many brushes use nylon or other synthetic fibres instead.

Indian miniature painters made some of the finest brushes of all. For the tiny details in [[@mughal-miniatures|Mughal miniatures]], artists used brushes made from just a few hairs, traditionally taken from a squirrel's tail or a kitten's fur. With them they could paint single eyelashes on a face no bigger than a fingernail.

text: Most of the sounds in a film aren't recorded while the cameras roll. They're added later by sound designers and Foley artists. Sound designers invent big sounds that don't exist in real life, like spaceship engines or dinosaur roars, often by mixing several real sounds together. Foley artists perform small everyday sounds, like footsteps, rustling clothes and doors, while watching the film on a screen.
Many of these sounds come from unlikely places. A punch might be a fist hitting a cabbage. Breaking bones are often snapped celery. Bird wings are a pair of leather gloves flapped in the air.

st.reveal: Squeezing a pouch of cornflour makes a soft, squeaky crunch that sounds just like boots in snow. Microphones can't tell the difference, and neither can audiences.

sec.t:
A film set is full of noise: generators, crew whispering, traffic outside. [[@microphones|Microphones]] are aimed at actors' mouths, so they catch voices well but quieter sounds badly. And some things can't be recorded at all. Nobody has ever heard a real dragon, a laser blast or a starship.

So after filming, the picture goes to a team who rebuild the sound, layer by layer. A single action scene can hold hundreds of separate sounds.

For the 1993 film *Jurassic Park*, sound designer Gary Rydstrom built the T. rex roar from a baby elephant's scream, a tiger and an alligator, slowed down and mixed. Nobody knows what a real T. rex sounded like. Some scientists think big [[@dino-sounds|dinosaurs]] may have made deep booming calls with their mouths closed, more like a pigeon's coo than a roar.

For *Star Wars* in 1977, Ben Burtt made the lightsaber hum from the idling motor of old cinema projectors. He added a buzz caught by accident when his microphone passed near a television set. Chewbacca's voice mixed recordings of bears, a walrus and other animals.

Cartoons need sounds that are bigger than life: a boing when a character bounces, a slide whistle when someone falls off a cliff. Early animation studios built their own libraries of these effects, and many are still used.

Video games need thousands of sounds that change as you play. A single footstep might be recorded on dozens of surfaces, so the game can pick the right one whether your character is walking on grass, metal, wood or snow.

One famous scream was recorded for a 1951 American film called *Distant Drums*. It ended up in a sound library and has since been used in hundreds of films and video games, often as a hidden joke among sound editors. It's called the Wilhelm scream, after a character named Private Wilhelm in a 1953 film who let it out after being hit by an arrow.

Sound designers also have to decide when to break the rules. Real space is silent, because there's no air to carry sound to your [[@ears-hear|ears]]. But a spaceship battle with no noise feels wrong to most audiences, so films add explosions anyway. If you want to know what space is really like, start with the strange truth about [[@space-weird-sound|sound in space]].

text: Museums exist to keep things that matter, so that people long after us can still see them. A museum collects objects, looks after them, studies them and puts them on show. A [[fossil|fossil]], a sword, a sari, a painting or a spacecraft can each teach something that a book can only describe.

The first museums were private collections owned by kings, priests and rich families. Over the last 300 years, they slowly opened their doors to everyone. Today there are tens of thousands of museums around the world, from giant national museums to a single room in a village.
Museums also argue about hard questions, such as who really owns the treasures they hold.

sec.t:
In about 530 BCE, in the ancient city of Ur in what is now Iraq, a princess named Ennigaldi-Nanna kept a collection of objects that were already centuries old. When the [[archaeologist|archaeologist]] Leonard Woolley dug there in the 1920s, he found the objects together, along with a clay label describing some of them in three languages. Some historians call it the world's first museum.

The word "museum" comes from Ancient Greek and means "place of the Muses", the goddesses of the arts and learning. In Alexandria, in Egypt, the Mouseion was a great centre for scholars, and it included the famous [[@great-libraries|library]] that collected scrolls from all over the known world.

sec.h: From private rooms to public halls
sec.t:
For centuries, collections stayed private. Wealthy Europeans in the 1500s and 1600s filled "cabinets of curiosities" with shells, stuffed animals, coins and carvings to impress their guests. In 1683, the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford opened as one of the first museums the public could visit.

The British Museum in [[@london|London]] was founded in 1753, built around the collection of a doctor named Hans Sloane. It promised free entry to "all studious and curious persons". After the [[@french-revolution|French Revolution]], the royal palace of the Louvre in [[@paris|Paris]] became a public museum in 1793. Today it holds the [[@mona-lisa|Mona Lisa]] and welcomes millions of visitors a year.

The British scientist James Smithson died in 1829. In his will, he left his fortune to the United States "to found at Washington, under the name of the Smithsonian Institution, an establishment for the increase and diffusion of knowledge". He had never set foot in America, and nobody knows exactly why he did it.

[[@smithsonian|The Smithsonian]] was founded in 1846. It now runs more than twenty museums and a zoo, most of them free to visit. Its National Air and Space Museum displays the [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]]' 1903 flyer, the first powered aeroplane to carry a pilot.

Many great museums in Europe and North America hold objects that were taken from other countries during wars or [[colonial|colonial]] rule. Some, like the [[@ancient-africa|Benin Bronzes]] from what is now [[@nigeria|Nigeria]], were seized by soldiers in 1897. Others were bought, given or dug up under rules that would not be allowed today.

Some people argue these objects should go home to the communities they came from. Others say big museums let millions of people see the art of many cultures in one place. In recent years, several museums and governments have returned objects. In 2022, Germany handed some of its Benin Bronzes back to Nigeria. The debate continues, one object at a time.

text: Qawwali is a form of devotional music from South Asia, sung by Sufis, Muslims who seek a deep, personal love of God. It is usually performed by a group: one or two lead singers, a chorus that sings back and claps, a harmonium player and a drummer on tabla or dholak.

The songs are poems of love and longing for God, or praise for the Prophet Muhammad and for Sufi saints. A qawwali starts slowly and gently, then builds through repetition, louder clapping and faster [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]] until it reaches a powerful climax. The word comes from the Arabic *qaul*, meaning a saying. For centuries it has been sung at Sufi shrines in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, and today it fills concert halls around the world.

st.reveal: The chorus sits behind the lead singers and claps hard on the beat. Their clapping is a real part of the music, and it gets faster and louder as the song builds.

n.certNote: Tradition credits the poet Amir Khusrau with creating qawwali around 1300. Historians agree he shaped it, but many think it grew gradually from older Sufi music gatherings rather than being invented by one person.

sec.t:
A qawwali often begins with an unaccompanied verse, sung freely without a beat. Then the [[@harmonium|harmonium]] picks up the tune, the drums come in and the chorus starts clapping. The lead singer takes one line of the poem and repeats it many times, stretching words and decorating the melody.

Each repetition pushes a little higher and a little faster. Listeners call out in appreciation, and some may sway or weep. The aim is to bring the audience into a state of spiritual joy, sometimes called *wajd*, a kind of ecstasy. In a shrine, people offer money to the singers as a sign of respect.

Qawwali poetry is full of images of love: the lover and the beloved, wine, the moth drawn to a candle. For Sufis, these stand for the soul's love of God. The poems are sung in Urdu, Persian, Punjabi, Hindi, the old Braj language and other tongues. Many were written by famous poets such as Khusrau, Bulleh Shah and Rumi.

Because the lead singer chooses which lines to repeat and how, no two performances of a song are quite the same.

In the 1980s and 1990s, the Pakistani singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan took qawwali to audiences across Europe, America and Japan. He worked with Western musicians and film-makers, and people who understood none of the words found themselves moved by his voice. The Sabri Brothers, also from Pakistan, were another famous group.

Hindi films have used qawwali for decades. [[@ar-rahman|A.R. Rahman]] composed "Kun Faya Kun" for the 2011 film *Rockstar*, and its video was filmed at the Nizamuddin shrine. In the United States, qawwali groups now perform at [[@festivals-music|music festivals]] and universities.

At many Sufi shrines, Hindus, Sikhs, Christians and Muslims sit side by side to listen. The [[@tabla|harmonium and tabla]] are the same instruments heard at a [[@devotional-music|bhajan]] or a classical concert. Many listeners, of every faith or none, say that qawwali speaks to them even when they cannot follow every word.

text: A snail's shell grows with the snail. It doesn't swap it for a bigger one the way a hermit crab does. Instead, a soft layer of its body called the mantle lays down new shell along the rim of the opening. The new material is mostly calcium carbonate, the same [[mineral|mineral]] that makes chalk.

The trick is that the mantle adds a little more on one side than the other. Each new ring is slightly wider than the last and slightly twisted. Keep doing that for months and the tube curls around itself. The result is a spiral, with the oldest, tiniest part at the tip and the newest part at the mouth.

st.reveal: The hatchling shell, called the protoconch, is never thrown away. All new shell is added at the opening, so the oldest, smallest part always sits at the point of the spiral.

sec.h: A spiral that keeps its shape
sec.t:
Mathematicians call this shape a logarithmic spiral. Its special property is that it grows without changing shape. A small piece near the tip looks just like a big piece near the opening, only scaled up.

That suits a growing animal well. A young snail and an old snail of the same kind have the same proportions, so the soft body inside always fits. Compare a coiled rope, where every turn sits the same distance from the last. Its outer turns would be far too tight for an animal that keeps getting bigger.

The tiny shell the snail hatched with, called the protoconch, stays at the very tip for life. In 1917 the Scottish [[biologist|biologist]] D'Arcy Thompson showed in his book On Growth and Form that horns, tusks and shells follow the same rule. Add at one end, never remodel the old part, and a spiral appears.

Hold most snail shells with the point up and the opening facing you, and the opening sits on the right. About 9 out of 10 snail [[species|species]] coil this way. Biologists call them dextral, or right-handed.

Left-handed snails do exist, but in a right-handed species they are very rare. In 2016 a left-coiling garden snail turned up in London. Scientists named him Jeremy and asked the public to find him a mate, because a left-coiler's body doesn't line up easily with a right-coiler's. Two more left-coilers were found. Their babies, and Jeremy's, all coiled to the right.

In India, the conch blown in temples, the shankha, is the shell of a sea snail from the Gulf of Mannar. A rare chank that coils the opposite way, called valampuri, is treasured.

You may read that shells follow the [[@golden-ratio|golden ratio]], a number close to 1.618 that people like to find in art and buildings. It's a lovely idea, but the measurements disagree. A golden spiral widens by 1.618 every quarter turn. Real nautilus shells widen much more slowly than that.

Different snails simply use different growth rates. A tall, pointed tower snail stretches its spiral downwards like a drill bit. A flat ramshorn snail from a pond coils almost like a jalebi. They all follow the same rule. Only the numbers change.

You can see the rule in action on a shell you find. The lines running across it, from the rim back towards the tip, are growth lines. Each one marks an old edge of the opening, a bit like rings in a tree trunk. Count them and you are reading the snail's diary.

text: A number pattern, or sequence, is a list of numbers that follows a rule. Spot the rule and you can predict every number that comes next, even the millionth one.

Some rules are simple. In 5, 10, 15, 20 you keep adding 5. In 1, 3, 9, 27 you keep multiplying by 3. Others are sneakier, like 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, which are the [[@triangular-numbers|square numbers]]. Mathematicians love patterns because finding one usually means something deeper is going on underneath.

sec.t:
[[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] poetry is built from short and long [[syllable|syllables]], a bit like short and long beats in music. Around 2,000 years ago, the scholar Pingala studied how many different [[rhythm|rhythms]] you could make from them.

Later writers, including Virahanka (around the 7th century) and Hemachandra (12th century), asked a neat question. If a short beat lasts one unit and a long beat lasts two, how many rhythms fill a line of a given length? The answers ran 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13: each number is the sum of the two before.

In 1202, Leonardo of Pisa, nicknamed Fibonacci, used the same numbers in a puzzle about breeding rabbits. Europe named them after him. The pattern also turns up in pine cones and sunflower heads, as [[@fibonacci-nature|Fibonacci in nature]] explains.

A well-known legend links this to [[@chess-india|chess]], whose earliest known form, chaturanga, comes from India. The inventor, it says, asked a king for one grain of rice on the first square of the board. He wanted two on the second, four on the third, and so on, [[@exponents|doubling each time]]. The king laughed at such a small reward. By the 64th square, the total would be more rice than the whole world grows in centuries.

The story is a legend, but the maths is real. Doubling patterns start slowly and then explode. Scientists see the same shape when [[bacteria|bacteria]] multiply or when a video spreads online. Fold a sheet of paper in half again and again, and its thickness doubles each time too, which is why you can rarely fold it more than seven or eight times.

sec.h: How to hunt for a rule
sec.t:
When you meet a new sequence, try a few tests. Look at the gaps between numbers. If the gaps are equal, you're adding. If they grow, look at the gaps between the gaps. Then try dividing each number by the one before. A steady answer means you're multiplying.

Some patterns resist every test. The [[@prime-numbers|prime numbers]] (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13) follow no simple rule that anyone has found, even though mathematicians have chased one for over 2,000 years. That stubbornness is part of what keeps them interested.

text: Most people make about half a litre to a litre and a half of saliva a day. That's somewhere between a small water bottle and a big one, every single day. Over a lifetime, it adds up to tens of thousands of litres, roughly enough to fill a couple of the water tankers you see on Indian streets.

Saliva is about 99% water, but the other 1% is busy. It contains an [[enzyme|enzyme]] that starts digesting [[starch|starch]], slippery substances that help you swallow, minerals that repair your teeth, and germ fighters. You make most of it when you eat, a little all day, and very little when asleep.

Dogs and humans each carry hundreds of kinds of bacteria in their mouths, many of them different. A dog's mouth isn't cleaner, it just has different germs. Washing your hands and face after a dog licks you is a good idea.

an enzyme that starts breaking down starch, and substances that fight germs

sec.t:
You have three big pairs of salivary [[gland|glands]]. The largest sit just in front of your ears. Another pair sits under your jaw, and the smallest pair under your tongue. Hundreds of tiny glands dot the lining of your mouth too.

The glands work harder when you smell, see or even think about food. Picture biting into a sour lemon or a raw mango with salt and chilli, and you may feel your mouth water right now. That is your brain switching on the glands before any food arrives.

Saliva begins breaking down food before you swallow. Its enzyme, amylase, chops starch from rice, roti and potatoes into smaller sugars. That's why chewing plain bread for a long time makes it taste sweet.

Saliva also wets and softens food so it slides down your throat as a soft ball. Without it, swallowing a dry biscuit would feel like swallowing sand. The rest of the journey is the story of [[@digestion-gut|your gut]].

Saliva also matters for taste. Flavour chemicals have to [[dissolve|dissolve]] before the [[@tongue-taste|taste buds]] on your tongue can detect them.

{{story:tongue-taste}}

After you eat, mouth [[bacteria|bacteria]] make [[acid|acids]] that attack your teeth. Saliva washes away bits of food, weakens the acid and carries minerals like calcium that help repair tiny damage to the enamel.

At night, saliva slows down a lot. Bacteria have a party, which is one reason for morning breath. It's also why brushing before bed matters so much for [[@teeth|teeth]].

Saliva also contains lysozyme, a substance that breaks open some bacteria. Alexander Fleming discovered it in 1921, a few years before he discovered penicillin.

Plenty of animals use spit in clever ways. Some swiftlets in South-East Asia and the Andaman Islands build their nests almost entirely from their own hardened saliva. People collect these nests to make an expensive soup, which has made some swiftlets [[endangered|endangered]].

Dogs drool when they expect food. In the early 1900s, the Russian scientist Ivan Pavlov studied this and found dogs would drool at sounds they linked with food, a famous discovery about learning. Vampire bats have saliva that stops blood from clotting while they feed.

Some medicines, illness and stress can cause a dry mouth, which makes talking, eating and tasting hard. Doctors can also test saliva instead of blood for some illnesses, because it carries traces of many things in the body.

Saliva even shows up when your body is about to empty your stomach. Just before throwing up, your mouth floods with extra spit to protect your teeth, part of the strange drill of [[@gross-vomit|vomiting]].

text: A joint is a place where bones meet. Without joints, your skeleton would be one stiff piece, and you couldn't walk, write or wave.

Most of the joints that move are built the same way. The ends of the bones are covered with smooth, slippery [[cartilage|cartilage]]. The joint is wrapped in a capsule filled with a thick, clear liquid called synovial fluid, which works like oil in a machine. Tough straps called [[ligament|ligaments]] hold the bones together, while [[@muscles|muscles]] attached by [[tendon|tendons]] pull on the bones to make them move.

sec.t:
Different joints move in different ways, and engineers recognise many of them from machines.

Your knees and elbows are hinge joints. Like a door hinge, they mostly bend and straighten in one direction. Your hips and shoulders are ball-and-socket joints: a rounded bone end sits in a cup, letting the arm or leg swing round in almost any direction.

When you shake your head to say no, you use a pivot joint between the top two bones of your neck. The joint at the base of your thumb is a saddle joint, which lets the thumb swing across to touch each fingertip. Small gliding joints in your wrists and ankles let bones slide over each other.

Some joints barely move at all. The bones of your skull are joined by wiggly seams that lock them in place to protect your brain.

Many children are told that cracking their knuckles will give them arthritis. An American doctor named Donald Unger decided to test it on himself. For more than 60 years, he cracked the knuckles of his left hand but not his right. In 1998 he reported that neither hand had arthritis. Larger studies have also found no link. His patient experiment earned him an Ig Nobel Prize in 2009, a jokey award for research that makes people laugh and then think.

The pop itself comes from the synovial fluid. When you pull the joint apart, a gas-filled space suddenly opens up in the fluid. Researchers in Canada filmed it inside a finger with an MRI scanner in 2015.

Joints like to move. Activity keeps the muscles around them strong, and strong muscles take strain off the joints. Sports like swimming, cycling and [[@gymnastics|gymnastics]] help keep joints flexible.

Sprains happen when a ligament is stretched too far, often at the ankle. Warming up before sport, wearing proper shoes and not playing through sharp pain all help. If a joint swells up badly or won't move after a fall, tell an adult so a doctor can take a look.

text: A reusable rocket brings its biggest part, the first stage or booster, back to Earth instead of letting it crash into the sea. After pushing the upper stage towards space, the booster separates, turns around and fires its engines again to fly back. Near the ground it fires once more to slow from hundreds of kilometres per hour to almost zero, then lowers four legs and touches down.

The first orbital-class booster to land like this was a SpaceX Falcon 9 in [[@usa-wonder-cape-canaveral|Florida]], on 21 December 2015. Since then, landings have become routine. The point is cost: building a rocket and then throwing it away after one flight is like scrapping an aeroplane after every trip.

st.reveal: The booster turns around and does a "boostback burn" to reverse direction. Later it fires again to slow down through the thick air, steers with small fins and lights one engine for the final landing.

NASA's Space Shuttle was reused from 1981. Its orbiter and its two side boosters flew again and again, though they needed months of costly repairs. Falcon 9 was the first orbital-class booster to land upright and be flown again regularly.

sec.h: Turning around at the edge of space
sec.t:
About two and a half minutes after launch, the Falcon 9 booster is roughly 70 km up and moving fast. It separates from the upper stage. Small gas thrusters flip it around, and a few engines fire to slow it and push it back towards land. This is the boostback burn.

The booster then falls, engines first. Four metal grid fins pop out near the top, like waffle-shaped flaps, to steer through the air. As it hits the thicker [[atmosphere|atmosphere]], the engines fire again in the entry burn to stop it from overheating.

[[@parachutes|Parachutes]] are used for capsules carrying astronauts, and some companies have tried them for boosters. But a booster is heavy and fragile when empty, and splashing into salty seawater damages its engines. Landing on legs on a dry pad means it can be checked, refuelled and flown again within weeks.

The Space Shuttle, which flew from 1981 to 2011, was partly reusable. It landed like a [[@gliders|glider]] on a runway, and its side boosters parachuted into the sea to be fished out. But each flight needed months of repairs, so it never became as cheap as hoped.

SpaceX's giant Starship goes further. In October 2024, its booster flew back to the launch tower in Texas and was caught in mid-air by two huge mechanical arms. Blue Origin, another American company, landed its small [[@space-tourism|New Shepard rocket]] a month before the first Falcon 9 landing, though New Shepard only makes short hops to space and straight back down.

ISRO is testing a winged spaceplane called the RLV, nicknamed Pushpak, after a flying chariot in the Ramayana. In 2023 and 2024, it was dropped from a helicopter at Challakere in [[@karnataka|Karnataka]] and glided down to land on a runway by itself. ISRO hopes a full-size version will one day [[@isro-launch|launch]] [[@satellites-help|satellites]] and fly back like a plane, ready for another trip to the edge of space.

text: Abraham Lincoln was the 16th President of the United States. He led the country through the [[@us-civil-war|Civil War]] of 1861–1865, when southern states tried to break away to protect slavery.

Lincoln held the country together, and the war ended with slavery abolished across the USA. He was killed just days after the main fighting stopped. He is remembered for his honesty and his gift with words. He believed a nation built on the idea that "all men are created equal" could not stay half slave and half free. People who met him often mentioned his jokes and stories, which he used to make a point or calm a tense room.

st.prompt: Lincoln's Gettysburg Address is one of the most famous speeches in history. How long did it take him to give it?
st.reveal: The speech has around 270 words and took about two minutes. The main speaker that day, Edward Everett, talked for about two hours. Almost nobody remembers his speech.

myth: Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation freed every enslaved person in the USA in 1863.

It applied only to states fighting against the Union, where Lincoln had no power to enforce it at first. Slavery ended everywhere in the country only with the 13th Amendment to the Constitution in December 1865.

sec.h: The boy in the log cabin
sec.t:
Lincoln was born in 1809 in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky. His family moved to Indiana and later to Illinois, clearing forest to farm. He split logs for fences, which later earned him the nickname "the Rail-Splitter".

His schooling added up to about a year, in short stretches. Books were rare on the frontier, so he borrowed whatever he could find, including the Bible and a history of George Washington. He read while walking behind the plough.

{{story:libraries}}

As a young man he ran a village shop, worked as a postmaster and steered a flatboat of goods down the [[@mississippi|Mississippi River]] to [[@new-orleans|New Orleans]]. He taught himself law and became a lawyer in Springfield, Illinois.

Lincoln served in the Illinois legislature and one term in the [[@congress-usa|US Congress]]. In 1858 he ran for the Senate against Stephen Douglas. Their debates about whether slavery should spread to new western lands drew huge crowds. Lincoln lost that race, but people across the country now knew his name.

In 1860 he was elected president. He opposed spreading slavery, and southern states feared he would end it altogether. Before he even took office, seven states left the Union. In April 1861, fighting began.

The Civil War was the deadliest war in American history. Around 6 to 7 lakh soldiers died, more than in any other war the country has fought.

At first, Lincoln said his main aim was to keep the country united. As the war went on, he decided that ending slavery was both right and necessary to win. On 1 January 1863, he issued the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring enslaved people in the rebel states free. Black soldiers could now join the Union army, and almost 2 lakh did.

In July 1863, a huge battle was fought at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. In November, Lincoln spoke at the opening of a cemetery there. His speech lasted about two minutes. He said the nation must make sure that "government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth."

Lincoln was re-elected in 1864. He pushed Congress to pass the 13th Amendment to the [[@us-constitution|Constitution]], banning slavery for good. The main southern army surrendered on 9 April 1865.

Five days later, on 14 April, Lincoln was shot while watching a play at Ford's Theatre in Washington. He died the next morning. The 13th Amendment became law that December, ending [[@slavery-freedom|slavery in the USA]].

Lincoln's face is on the US five-dollar note, and on [[@mount-rushmore|Mount Rushmore]]. In Washington, D.C., a giant statue of him sits inside the Lincoln Memorial, completed in 1922.

text: Assam became famous for tea because a strong, native kind of tea plant grows there naturally, and the British turned that discovery into one of the world's biggest tea industries. The plant loves Assam's [[climate|climate]]: hot, humid summers, very heavy [[@monsoon|monsoon]] rain and rich soil along the [[@brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]] river.

Today Assam grows about half of all India's tea. Its tea is dark and malty, strong enough to stand up to milk and sugar. That's why it goes into so many breakfast teas in Britain and the United States, and into countless cups of [[@food-chai-history|chai]] at Indian railway stations and roadside stalls.

st.prompt: In the early 1800s, almost all the tea drunk in Britain came from one country. Which one?
st.reveal: China controlled the tea trade and kept its methods secret. The British wanted their own supply, so the discovery of a native tea plant in Assam, inside land they were taking over, was big news.

n.certNote: Tea from Assam is well documented. Who "discovered" it is told differently. British records credit Robert Bruce and his brother Charles, but the Singpho people were already brewing the wild leaves long before.

sec.h: A plant hiding in plain sight
sec.t:
In the early 1800s, Britain drank huge amounts of tea, nearly all of it from China. China guarded its tea secrets closely. Paying for it in silver was costly, and that trade became part of the story of the [[@opium-wars|Opium Wars]].

In 1823, a Scottish trader named Robert Bruce was told about wild tea growing in Assam by a Singpho chief called Bessa Gam. The Singpho people had been brewing its leaves for generations. After Robert died, his brother Charles Bruce carried on the work, collecting plants and seeds and setting up the first experimental gardens.

British [[botanist|botanists]] at first doubted that this was real tea. Eventually they agreed it was a variety of the same plant, now called *Camellia sinensis* var. *assamica*. Its leaves are bigger than those of Chinese tea, and it grows into a small tree if left unpruned.

{{story:east-india-company}}

In 1839, the first Assam tea was auctioned in London, and the Assam Company was formed to grow it. Forests were cleared, and neat rows of bushes spread across the valley. Gardens were laid out on gentle slopes and plains, with tall shade trees dotted between the bushes.

An Assamese nobleman, Maniram Dewan, worked with the early British companies and later set up gardens of his own. He is remembered as one of the first Indian tea planters. In 1858, the British executed him for supporting the revolt of 1857.

Tea needs many hands. Leaves are plucked by hand, usually just "two leaves and a bud" from each shoot, every week or so. From the 1800s, British companies brought hundreds of thousands of workers, many of them Adivasi people from central and eastern India, to work in the gardens.

Conditions were often harsh: low pay, crowded housing and contracts that made it hard to leave. Their [[descendant|descendants]] still make up much of the workforce on Assam's tea estates. Pay and living conditions remain a big issue today. Their music and dances, such as the jhumur, have become part of Assam's culture too.

After plucking, leaves are withered, rolled or crushed, left to darken in the air, and then dried. Most Assam tea is made by a method called CTC (crush, tear, curl), which turns leaves into tiny dark granules. These brew fast and strong, perfect for [[@tea|chai]] boiled with milk.

Some gardens make finer, whole-leaf teas with golden tips, which sell for high prices. Tea gardens border wildlife areas like [[@rhino-kaziranga|Kaziranga]], where one-horned rhinos and elephants roam. Sometimes elephants wander through the tea rows at night, and workers arrive in the morning to find their footprints between the bushes.

text: Rani ki Vav, or the Queen's Stepwell, is a giant well in Patan, Gujarat, with seven levels of stone steps leading down to water. It was built around 1063 CE. It is about 64 m long, longer than half a football field, and goes down about 27 m, as deep as a nine-storey building is tall.

Its walls and pillars are covered in more than 500 large carvings of gods, goddesses and dancers, plus over 1,000 smaller ones. It is often called the "queen of stepwells". In 2014 it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

As swimming pools for the royal family
To keep enemy armies out of the city

st.reveal: In dry western India, rain falls mostly in a few monsoon months. Stepwells let people walk down to groundwater all year. They were also cool, shady places to rest, meet and pray.

myth: Rani ki Vav was built by a king in honour of his queen.
It was the other way round. Historians believe Queen Udayamati built it in memory of her husband, King Bhimadeva I. That is why it is called the Queen's Stepwell.

sec.h: Why build a palace for water?
sec.t:
In much of Gujarat and Rajasthan, almost all the year's rain falls in the [[monsoon|monsoon]]. For the rest of the year, rivers dry up. But water still sits underground, soaking through sand and rock.

[[@stepwells|Stepwells]] let people reach that [[@groundwater|groundwater]] without ropes or buckets. You walked down the steps as far as the water level that season. When the water was high after the rains, the upper steps were enough. In the dry season, you went deeper. Stepwells stayed several degrees cooler than the hot streets above, so they were also places to rest and chat.

Many of the carvings show the ten avatars of Vishnu, including Rama, Krishna, Narasimha and Vamana. Vishnu also appears reclining on the serpent Shesha, floating on the cosmic ocean.

There are also *apsaras*, heavenly dancers, shown putting on make-up, fixing earrings or looking into mirrors. Some patterns on the walls look like the designs on Patola saris, the famous double-ikat silks still woven in Patan today.

Not long after it was built, the nearby Saraswati river flooded again and again. Mud and silt poured into the stepwell and slowly filled it up. For centuries, only the top of the well could be seen.

In the 1940s, digging in Baroda State began to show what was underneath. Excavation and restoration by the Archaeological Survey of India, mostly in the 1980s, cleared out the silt, level by level. Because the mud had covered the carvings for so long, many were protected from wind and rain. That is why so many look sharp after 900 years.

Local stories say a tunnel at the bottom of the well once led about 30 km to the town of Sidhpur, perhaps as an escape route for the royal family. The tunnel is said to be blocked with stones and mud. Nobody has proved it exists, so treat it as a legend.

In 2018, the Reserve Bank of India issued a new lavender ₹100 note with Rani ki Vav on the back. So many Indians carry a picture of it without knowing.

Rani ki Vav is among the finest of thousands of stepwells across western India. Several famous ones were paid for by queens and other women, as gifts to their towns. Some fell out of use when piped water and borewells arrived, and filled with rubbish. Others are now being cleaned and used again to store rainwater. The most dizzying of all may be [[@india-wonder-chand-baori|Chand Baori]] in Rajasthan, where about 3,500 steps zigzag down into the earth.

text: Urdu grew out of the everyday speech of the region around Delhi, starting roughly 800 years ago. When Turkic and Persian-speaking rulers set up the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] in the 1200s, soldiers, traders and officials needed a common tongue. Local speech borrowed thousands of words from Persian, Arabic and Turkic.

Over centuries this mixed language became a rich literary language, written in the Perso-Arabic [[script|script]]. Its flowing Nastaliq letters slant from upper right to lower left, and each letter changes shape depending on its neighbours. That made Urdu hard to set in metal type, so many Urdu newspapers were copied out by hand by calligraphers until computers learned the style in the 1980s. Today it is the national language of Pakistan and one of India's 22 scheduled languages.

st.reveal: Kitaab and duniya come from Arabic, and zindagi from Persian, mostly through Urdu. Spoken Hindi and Urdu share thousands of such words, which is why speakers of each understand the other easily.

myth: Urdu came to India from Arabia or Persia.

Urdu grew up inside India. Its grammar and most basic words come from the speech of the Delhi region. Persian and Arabic gave it much vocabulary, but it was born in Indian cities and camps, and spoken by people of many faiths.

sec.t:
For a long time the language had no fixed name. People called it Hindavi, Hindi, Dehlavi or Rekhta, which means "scattered" or "mixed". The name Urdu came later. It is short for a phrase meaning "the language of the exalted camp", referring to the royal city of Delhi.

The poet Amir Khusrau, who lived around 1300, wrote mostly in Persian but also composed riddles and songs in Hindavi. Many people see him as an early voice of the language.

Surprisingly, some of the earliest Urdu poetry was written far from Delhi, in the kingdoms of the Deccan such as Golconda and Bijapur. There it was called Dakhani. In about 1700 a poet known as Wali Dakhani visited Delhi, and his verses made Delhi's own poets take the language seriously.

{{story:mughals}}

In the 18th and 19th centuries, Urdu poetry flowered in Delhi and Lucknow, even as Mughal power faded. The favourite form was the [[@ghazals|ghazal]], a poem of linked [[couplet|couplets]] about love and loss. Mir Taqi Mir and Mirza Ghalib are the giants. Ghalib's old house in Ballimaran, a narrow lane in Old Delhi, is now a small museum.

Later, Muhammad Iqbal wrote "Saare Jahan Se Achha" in 1904. It is still sung by Indian schoolchildren, and its tune is played at the Beating Retreat ceremony after Republic Day.

sec.h: Hindi and Urdu: twins with two scripts
sec.t:
In everyday speech Hindi and Urdu are very close. Their grammar is almost the same, and a Hindi speaker in Lucknow and an Urdu speaker in Karachi can chat easily. Linguists often call the shared spoken language Hindustani. The big differences are the script, Devanagari or Nastaliq, and the formal vocabulary. Formal Hindi borrows from [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]], while formal Urdu borrows from Persian and Arabic.

In the 19th century, under British rule, the two drifted apart as each was linked with a religious community. That division hardened at the [[@partition|Partition of India]] in 1947. Yet the great writer [[@premchand|Premchand]] began writing his stories in Urdu before switching to Hindi.

If you watch [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] films, you already know a lot of Urdu. Words like ishq, khwaab and mohabbat fill [[@film-songs|film songs]], because lyricists such as Sahir Ludhianvi and Gulzar have drawn heavily on Urdu poetry. India's 2011 [[@census|Census]] counted about 5 crore Urdu speakers, with large communities in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Telangana and Maharashtra. Several states, including Telangana, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, use it as an official language alongside another. Many more people use its words every day without thinking about where they came from.

text: Food goes bad mainly because tiny [[microbe|microbes]], such as [[bacteria|bacteria]] and moulds, grow on it. To grow, they need water, warmth and time. So every old way of keeping food fresh takes away one of those things.

Drying removes water. Salt and sugar soak water up, leaving microbes thirsty. Pickling in [[acid|acid]] or oil makes food a hostile place to live. Smoke coats food with chemicals that slow germs down. And cold, from cellars, snow or carried ice, slows everything. People worked all of this out by trial and error, thousands of years before anyone saw a germ.

st.prompt: Fish packed in lots of salt can last for months. Why does salt stop it rotting?

options.t: Salt pulls water out, and spoiling microbes need water to grow
Salt freezes the fish from the inside
Salt is so heavy that it squashes the germs

st.reveal: Microbes that rot food need water. Salt and sugar soak water out of the food and out of the microbes themselves, so they cannot grow. That is why jams, murabbas and salted fish keep so long.

myth: In the Middle Ages, rich Europeans used spices to hide the taste of rotten meat.

Historians find little evidence for this. Spices were very expensive, and anyone who could afford pepper and cloves could also afford fresh meat. People bought spices for flavour, medicine and to show off.
facts: they pull water out of microbes

sec.t:
Drying is probably the oldest trick. Grapes become raisins, and fish and [[@mango-varieties|mango slices]] shrivel in the sun. In Indian homes, summer is still the season for drying [[@papad|papad]], vadi and sabudana chips on rooftops.

Salt goes further. Salted fish fed sailors on long voyages, and salted meat filled the barrels of armies. Native peoples of North America made pemmican, a mix of dried meat and fat that kept for months on long journeys. Smoking, often done alongside salting, gave hams and fish a flavour people came to love for its own sake.

A jar of Indian [[@pickles-achar|achar]] is a small [[fortress|fortress]]. Salt, oil, [[@mustard|mustard]] seeds and [[@chillies|chillies]] make it very hard for spoiling microbes to survive, and some pickles are also soured by friendly bacteria through [[@fermentation|fermentation]].

Sugar works in a similar way to [[@salt|salt]]. In a thick jam or a murabba of amla, there is so much sugar that microbes cannot pull water out of it. Vinegar pickles, popular in Europe and the United States, use acid instead.

India had its own cooling methods. Water kept in an unglazed clay [[@evaporation-cooling|matka]] stays cool because a little seeps through the walls and evaporates, carrying heat away. Curd and butter were often hung in pots in the shade or lowered into wells, where the air is cooler.

In some parts of north India and Persia, people even made ice in winter. They left water in shallow pits on clear, cold nights, and by dawn a thin skin of ice had formed. It was collected and stored in deep, insulated pits. Mughal emperors also had ice carried down from the mountains for cool drinks.

Around 1810 a French cook named Nicolas Appert found that food sealed in glass jars and then boiled could last for a very long time. The French government, keen to feed its armies, gave him a prize. Soon others were sealing food in [[@canned-food|tin cans]].

Appert did not know why his method worked. Decades later Louis Pasteur showed that heat kills microbes, and sealing keeps new ones out. Canned beans and tinned fish on a shop shelf today use the same idea.

Electric home [[@refrigerator|refrigerators]] became common in American homes from the 1920s onward, and spread more slowly in India in the decades after independence. Today the fridge does what cellars, snow and salt once did, mostly by slowing microbes down. But the older ways never vanished. Salted fish, dried mango and lime pickle are still made because people simply like the taste.
